name: Facial Toning Device (Bear)

card.summary: A handheld consumer microcurrent facial device marketed to tone and lift the look of the face with low-level electrical stimulation.
card.note: Not for use with pacemakers; manufacturer instructions govern use.

quick.overview:
The Bear facial toning device is a handheld microcurrent unit of the kind sold for home skincare. Microcurrent devices pass low-level current through the skin via metal probes or pads, and are marketed for a firmer, more lifted-looking face.

Users move the handset over facial contours after applying a conductive gel, and report a short-term toned look. Controlled research on this specific product was not found, and published research on electrical stimulation concentrates on muscle training and rehabilitation rather than facial appearance.[1]
quick.how: Typically a conductive gel is applied and the handset glided along the jawline, cheeks and brow in short regular sessions, following the maker's instructions.
quick.risks: Electrical stimulation devices list skin irritation and burns as potential adverse effects, and labelling excludes pacemaker wearers and use across the chest or head areas such as the carotid region.[1] The FDA and FTC have acted on unsubstantiated cosmetic claims for some consumer stimulation devices.[1]

lead: The Bear facial toning device is a handheld microcurrent gadget for home use, marketed to tone the face. Microcurrent devices apply low-level electrical current to facial skin and muscle; users aim for a firmer, lifted-looking contour.

General research on electrical muscle stimulation concerns strength training and rehabilitation, where low-certainty improvements have been reported, and cosmetic use is mentioned only in passing.[1] Regulators have taken action against consumer devices making body-shaping claims, so product claims differ by market.[1]

chain: Low-level current applied via handset over facial contours
Temporarily firmer-looking face, per users and makers
angle.text: Users apply it to the jaw, cheeks and brow hoping for a firmer, more lifted look. Effects described by marketers are short-term and are not documented in trials of this product.

paras: Microcurrent facial handsets are consumer versions of electrical stimulation equipment. Wikipedia notes that cosmetic use of electrical muscle stimulation appears in the field alongside training and rehabilitation uses.[1]

Labelling for stimulation devices bars use by pacemaker wearers and across the chest or brain; skin irritation and burns are listed as possible adverse effects; caution is also advised in pregnancy.[1]
No studies found. Studies of the broader category of electrical muscle stimulation focus on limb strength and report low-certainty improvements.[1]
